About: layers of fluid in a plane sound wave

Source

Concept
A plane harmonic sound wave in air (ρ₀ = 1.20 kg m⁻³, c = 343 m s⁻¹; f = 343 Hz, λ = 1.00 m, one period T = 2.92 ms; pressure amplitude 𝒜 = 1.00 Pa), linear and lossless. The top row plots the excess pressure p and the middle row the displacement ξ, both at their true values against the undisturbed position x from 0 to 2.00 m. The bottom row shows 33 layers of fluid above ticks marking where each sat before the wave arrived, their displacements magnified 85 000 times; the words "compression" and "rarefaction" sit under the maxima and minima of p.
Serves
Fermi Notes, §3.3 Longitudinal Waves in Bars and Fluids (Fig. 39) and §6.2 Plane and Spherical Sound Waves (Figs. 90–91): sound as a longitudinal wave, and the relations between displacement, excess pressure and particle velocity.
Inquiry
Four questions, then a closing summary card, about one layer, highlighted in purple with an arrow above it showing its velocity and a dashed line through all three rows. The readouts in the sidebar, below the controls, are measured at that layer's tick: the time t in periods T (one period, 2.92 ms, shown in 4 s at 1×), the tick position, ξ in μm, u in mm s⁻¹ and p in Pa. A dashed u curve on its own right-hand scale can join the top row.
Controls
Click any tick in the layer row to follow that layer. The direction of travel (towards +x or towards −x) can be switched at any instant; the phase carries on from its present value. ▶ Play / ⏸ Pause and Speed are in the header; Step ⅛ T advances the time by an eighth of a period and pauses; ⏮ Back to t = 0 returns to t = 0, paused, keeping the direction and the layer; the header ↻ Reset restores every default.
Misconception
Common ideas about where the fluid is squeezed and how the fluid in a compression moves; the questions let the readouts and the layer row decide.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Real values, honestly magnifiedAir at ρ₀ = 1.20 kg m⁻³, c = 343 m s⁻¹, 𝒜 = 1.00 Pa; p and ξ plotted at true values; only the layer row is magnified, and it says so beside the row; the slowed clock is stated at the foot of the Readouts panel.
Stable axesFixed scales of ±1.5 Pa and ±1.5 μm, and a right-hand u scale of ±1.5 times the velocity amplitude; nothing is ever rescaled.
Operational, not vibesFive readouts at the followed tick, at the precision the questions quote; exact zeros of the model print as 0.00 with no sign.
Evidence, not assertionNo captions explain how the curves relate; the student reads the curves, the layers and the readouts.
Sealed expert deckThe four SME questions, each gated, with feedback written for each answer choice; every question starts from the set-up its stem names; a closing card states the relations.
Control where the question needs it⏮ Back to t = 0, the direction selector and Step ⅛ T sit in the sidebar just above the readouts, pinned on screen while a card is open.
Layers of Fluid in a Plane Sound Wave
A plane sound wave in air against undisturbed position x

Guided Inquiry

1 · The layer displaced furthest

With the wave paused at t = 0 and travelling towards +x, click the tick of one of the layers displaced furthest towards +x. What are the excess pressure at that layer and its velocity?

2 · A layer in a compression

Click the tick at x = 1.00 m, which belongs to the layer in the middle of the compression at the centre of the layer row, then press play and follow that layer through a few periods. How is the layer moving each time a compression is centred on it?

3 · Stepping through a period

Press ⏮ Back to t = 0, keeping the layer at x = 1.00 m. Press Step ⅛ T, which advances the time by one eighth of a period, until the displacement of the layer reaches its largest positive value, and one step further. When is the layer displaced furthest forwards?

4 · Sending the wave the other way

Press ⏮ Back to t = 0, keeping the layer at x = 1.00 m. The top row now also shows the particle velocity u of every layer as a dashed curve, on the right-hand scale. Switch the direction of travel to −x, which runs the wave backwards from this instant. Which way does the fluid in each compression now move?

5 · Displacement, pressure and velocity

In a sound wave the excess pressure is set by how the displacement changes along x, p = −B ∂ξ/∂x. So the compressions and rarefactions sit where ξ passes through zero, a quarter of a wavelength from the layers displaced furthest, which are at ambient pressure and momentarily at rest. The particle velocity is in step with the pressure, u = ±p/ρ₀c, the sign set by the direction of travel: the fluid in a compression moves with the wave, the fluid in a rarefaction against it.

Layers of Fluid in a Plane Sound Wave

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A sound wave is not air rushing down the room. It is a pattern that travels through layers of air, each of which sways about its own place. This sim follows those layers through a plane wave in air.

What you'll learn

  • What one layer of air does as a sound wave passes.
  • How the displacement, the pressure and the velocity at a layer are linked.
  • What happens to each when the wave is sent the other way.
The three rows of the sim, shown empty, with the layer followed in purple.

What's on screen

  • Top row: the excess pressure p in Pa along x from 0 to 2.00 m. A dashed orange curve for the particle velocity u, on its own right-hand scale, can join it.
  • Middle row: the displacement ξ in μm. Both curves are at their true values.
  • Bottom row: 33 layers of fluid above ticks that mark where each sat before the wave arrived, drawn 85 000 times magnified. The words “compression” and “rarefaction” sit under the maxima and minima of p.
  • Readouts: at the followed layer, the time t in periods T, then ξ, u and p.
See itPress Play and watch the curves, the layers and the Readouts together. Watch for: the curves sliding to the right while the layers sway about their ticks, one period T taking 4 s on screen.

Fixed: air with ρ0 = 1.20 kg m−3 and c = 343 m s−1, a wave of f = 343 Hz and pressure amplitude 𝒜 = 1.00 Pa, linear and lossless. So λ = 1.00 m, and ρ0c = 411.6 Pa s m−1.

03

The layers sway about their ticks while the pattern travels at c

In a sound wave each thin layer of fluid is shifted a little from where it sat before the wave arrived, and back again. The notes call the shift ξ(x, t), for the layer whose rest position is x (§3.3). The sim marks every rest position with a tick.

What travels is the pattern. Here f = 343 Hz and c = 343 m s−1, so λ = c/f = 1.00 m and the period is T = 2.92 ms. In one period the pattern moves a whole wavelength, while each layer ends up back at its own tick.

The pattern travels; each layer only swings about its tick.

The layers hardly move: ξ reaches only 1.13 μm. The layer row is drawn about 85 000 times magnified so the sway can be seen. The two curves above it are at true scale.

See itPress Play and follow the purple layer. Watch for: the purple layer swinging to and fro about its tick while the pattern slides towards +x.
04

Pressure follows the slope of the displacement, not the displacement itself

A fluid resists being squeezed: a fractional volume change ΔV/V gives an excess pressure −B ΔV/V (3.26), with B the bulk modulus. A slice whose faces are displaced by different amounts is squeezed or stretched by the difference, so the pressure comes from the slope of ξ (3.27).

Notes (3.27). Here B = ρ0c2 = 1.41×105 Pa (3.29).

Where neighbouring layers are displaced by nearly equal amounts, the fluid is not squeezed and p = 0, however large ξ is there. The pressure is greatest where ξ passes through zero and falls with x, because layers on both sides are displaced towards that point (notes, Fig. 39).

At t = 0: p in Pa (blue) and ξ in μm.

At 0.75 m, ξ = +1.13 μm, its greatest, and p = 0.00 Pa. At 1.00 m, ξ = 0 and p = +1.00 Pa, the pressure amplitude 𝒜. They are a quarter of a wavelength apart.

See itFollow the layer at 0.75 m with the wave paused at t = 0. Watch for: the purple layer drawn to the right of its tick, with ξ = +1.13 μm and p = 0.00 Pa in the Readouts.
05

A compression moves the fluid forwards and a rarefaction moves it backwards

For a wave towards +x, ξ depends on x and t only through x − ct, so u = ∂ξ/∂t = −c ∂ξ/∂x. With p = −B ∂ξ/∂x and B = ρ0c2, this is (6.21):

Notes (6.21), for a wave towards +x. Here ρ0c = 411.6 Pa s m−1.

u has the sign of p. In a compression the fluid moves with the wave, in a rarefaction against it. At 1.00 m, p = +1.00 Pa gives u = +2.43 mm s−1, the greatest speed. At 0.50 m, in a rarefaction, u = −2.43 mm s−1.

At t = 0, towards +x: p and u share a shape; arrows show u.

At the centre of a compression the pushes from both sides are equal, so the acceleration is zero at that instant (3.28). That is not rest: the layer is passing the middle of its swing, where ξ = 0, at its greatest speed.

See itFollow the layer at 1.00 m at t = 0, then click the tick at 0.50 m. Watch for: p = +1.00 Pa with u = +2.43 mm s−1 at 1.00 m, then p = −1.00 Pa with u = −2.43 mm s−1 at 0.50 m.
06

The furthest displacement comes a quarter of a period after the compression

Follow the layer at 1.00 m. At t = 0 a compression is centred on it, with ξ = 0 and u = +2.43 mm s−1. The layer keeps moving forwards for as long as p stays positive, and p falls to zero a quarter of a period later.

The layer at 1.00 m, towards +x. Dots: t = 0, ⅛ T, ¼ T, ⅜ T.

At t = T/4 the compression has moved on a quarter of a wavelength, to 1.25 m. The layer is at the end of its swing, with ξ = +1.13 μm, p = 0.00 Pa and u = 0.00 mm s−1. The notes give the same lag: at a point, ξ is a quarter of a period behind p and u (§6.2).

Press Step ⅛ T from t = 0: ξ reads 0, +0.80, +1.13 and +0.80 μm at 0, ⅛, ¼ and ⅜ of a period. At ½ T a rarefaction is centred on the layer, with ξ = 0 again and p = −1.00 Pa.

See itFollow the layer at 1.00 m and step to t = ¼ T. Watch for: t = 0.250 T with ξ = +1.13 μm, and u and p both 0.00: the layer at the end of its swing.
07

Reversing the wave turns u over but leaves p and ξ as they were

Send the pattern towards −x and ξ depends on x + ct instead, so u = ∂ξ/∂t = +c ∂ξ/∂x = −p/ρ0c. The notes give the relation for both directions (6.21).

Notes (6.21): + towards +x, − towards −x.

At the instant of the switch, p and ξ depend only on the displacements and spacings, which have not changed. So at 1.00 m p = +1.00 Pa and ξ = 0 as before, and only u turns over, to −2.43 mm s−1. The fluid in a compression moves in the new direction of travel.

The same instant, two directions: p and ξ are identical, the arrows for u reverse.

What follows differs. The layer at 1.00 m now moves backwards, reaching ξ = −0.80 μm at ⅛ T and −1.13 μm at ¼ T, and the compression has moved on to 0.75 m.

See itSwitch to towards −x at t = 0, with the layer at 1.00 m. Watch for: u = −2.43 mm s−1 while p is still +1.00 Pa, and the dashed u curve upside down against the p curve.
08

Where it matters

  • Sound in air. A pressure amplitude of 1.00 Pa is a root-mean-square 0.71 Pa, a sound pressure level of 20 log10(0.71/2×10−5) = 91 dB (6.46). That is a loud sound.
  • Tiny motions. The layers sway 1.13 μm and move at 2.43 mm s−1, against c = 343 m s−1. The fractional squeeze is p/B = u/c = 7×10−6, which is why the linear relations hold. The drawing exaggerates it: neighbouring layers are drawn between 0.4 and 1.6 of their rest spacing.
  • The ratio ρ0c. It sets how much velocity a given pressure drives. It is 411.6 Pa s m−1 for this air, and the notes say several thousand times larger for water (6.23).
  • What is left out. The wave is plane, linear and lossless, so there is no spreading and no damping.
09

Summary

In one line. The sim follows layers of air through a plane sound wave and reads the displacement, the pressure and the velocity at one of them.

Key points

  • p = −B ∂ξ/∂x: pressure comes from the slope of the displacement.
  • u = ±p/ρ0c, the sign set by the direction of travel.
  • At a layer, ξ lags u by a quarter of a period; for a wave towards +x it also lags p by a quarter period (towards −x it leads p). Reversing the wave at an instant turns only u over.

Common mix-ups

  • “The layer that moved furthest is under the greatest pressure.” At 0.75 m, ξ = +1.13 μm and p = 0.00 Pa.
  • “A compression pushes the fluid backwards.” Towards +x, u = +2.43 mm s−1 where p = +1.00 Pa.
  • “In a compression the layer is at rest.” Equal pushes mean no acceleration, not no velocity.
  • “Reversing the wave reverses the pressure.” p and ξ stay; only u turns over.

Things to try on your own

  • Click the tick at 0.25 m at t = 0: ξ = −1.13 μm and p = 0.00 Pa.
  • Switch to towards −x, press Play and watch the layer at 1.00 m move backwards.
  • Set the Speed to 0.25× and play: u reaches zero just as ξ is greatest.
